I have been farming these 14 mu for 25 years, and I know every ridge and hollow. With six people in my household, I cannot afford gambles. My well gives me reliable water, which is more than some neighbors have, but diesel for the pump and fertilizer still cost real money. It is early spring now. My winter wheat went into the ground last October after I rotary-tilled the maize stubble. I use an improved wheat variety that has never let me down. This spring I will top-dress urea at green-up and again at jointing, bringing the season total to about 16 kg of nitrogen per mu, with another 6 kg phosphorus and 4 kg potassium from compound fertilizer. I will irrigate four times—now at green-up, then at jointing, at heading, and once more at grain filling if May turns dry. For protection, I will spray four times: herbicide first to stop weeds, then insecticide twice, and fungicide once against rust. I expect 500 kg per mu if frost stays away. Come early June, the day the wheat comes off, I will plant summer maize with no-tillage direct seeding; everyone here does it that way because it saves time and traps moisture. I will buy hybrid seed from the township shop—hybrids cost more but the yield jump pays for itself. For the maize I will put down compound fertilizer at planting and side-dress nitrogen at the big-flare stage, totaling about 15 kg nitrogen per mu, 5 kg phosphorus, and 4 kg potassium. I will irrigate twice, once knee-high and again at tasseling or filling if the rains hold off. Three sprays will do for maize: herbicide at planting and insecticide twice for corn borer. I am counting on 550 kg per mu from the hybrid. I keep my inputs steady because my family eats and sells from this same patch; after a quarter century, I trust what works.
